children: By Gavin Maguire

Natural gas was supposed to be the dominant bridge fuel between legacy generation systems and a clean-powered future. But across key markets in Europe and Asia, power producers appear to be increasingly bypassing the fuel in favour of other options.

Total electricity generation from gas-fired power plants has contracted this year from 2025 in the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, Turkey, Japan, South Korea and China, according to data from think tank Ember.

Those countries represent some of the key traditional and high-potential gas markets for gas power generation, and yet all simultaneously pared back gas use this year as global supplies and prices were impacted by the war in the Middle East.

Significantly, total electricity generation across those six nations has expanded this year despite lower collective gas-fired output, resulting in natural gas losing share to other generation sources within those key power networks.
For exporters of liquefied natural gas, the risk is that gas remains essential as a marginal fuel but ceases to be a growth engine for power generation.

Power systems still need gas-fired plants to bolster reliability, but they appear to need progressively less gas-fired electricity from those facilities as renewable generation, storage and output from other power sources expand.
That is a challenging outlook for an industry investing heavily in new export capacity on the assumption that tomorrow's power sector will burn substantially more gas than today's.
SHARE SQUEEZE
The steady erosion of natural gas' share within a wide span of key power sectors underscores the problem for gas market bulls.

In the Netherlands, home to Europe's main gas trading hub, the gas share of electricity generation during the first nine months of 2026 was just under 32%. That's the lowest reading on record for that period and compares to a nearly 60% gas share in the same months in 2020 and nearly 40% in 2022.

In the United Kingdom, the closure of the country's last remaining coal power plant in late 2024 was expected to trigger a sustained upturn in gas use. Yet gas' share of the utility mix plumbed a new low of 29% so far this year, compared to roughly 41% in the same months in 2022.
And in Turkey, which was long considered a viable growth market for gas due to its fast-growing manufacturing base, gas' share of the generation mix this year has dropped to just under 11%.

That compares to an average 32% gas share in 2021, which is when Turkey's gas-fired generation total hit a record and spurred optimism among gas exporters that the country would continue to steadily increase its gas needs.
Gas has also lost ground across key Asian markets.

In Japan, which for years has been one of the top LNG importers, gas use in electricity generation has lost ground to both rising output from renewables and a recovery in output from the country's nuclear reactor fleet.
The gas share of Japan's electricity mix so far this year was 28.4%, which was the first reading on record below 30%, and compares to an average share of around 35% in 2022 and nearly 40% in 2019.
South Korea's power system also reduced gas' share to a multi-year low of just under 29% this year, while in China gas' share of the mix was just 3.07%, which again was a record low.
ABSOLUTE PEAK?
For gas market bulls, the trends in absolute levels of gas-fired generation are also likely to be a cause for concern.
In all six of the key markets noted above, year-to-date generation from gas-fired power plants has posted a decline this year, just as output from many other sources has increased in 2026.
In Europe, higher output from renewables installations alongside battery storage networks has allowed most utilities to boost total electricity supplies while cutting overall gas generation.
In Turkey, a jump in hydro power production to the highest in over five years also allowed for lower gas consumption.

In Asia, power producers dialled up generation from cheaper coal-fired power stations to accommodate tighter gas supplies, which have been hampered by the US and Israeli war against Iran and the subsequent drops in LNG shipments from Qatar.
The worrying signal for LNG producers is that this decline has occurred even before a new wave of gas export capacity comes online.
Major suppliers are investing billions of dollars on the assumption that power demand growth will translate into rising gas consumption for decades to come.
Yet across several of the world's most important gas-burning economies, utilities are finding ways to grow electricity supplies while reducing reliance on gas-fired generation.
If that pattern spreads further, the industry's challenge may not be securing enough supply to meet future demand, but finding enough demand to absorb future supply.
Gas may remain indispensable in many modern power systems, but the latest generation trends suggest it is increasingly valued for reliability rather than volume.
That's an uncomfortable distinction for exporters betting on sustained growth.
